Investing.com - S&P 500 futures inched higher on Wednesday, while Nasdaq futures hovered below the flatline, as investors geared up for the release of key U.S. inflation data and a fresh batch of large bank earnings.
By 07:32 ET (11:32 GMT), S&P 500 futures had ticked up by 13 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq futures had edged down by 30 points, or 0.1%. Dow futures, meanwhile, gained 155 points, or 0.3%.
The main averages on Wall Street finished lower in the prior session, weighed down in part by lingering questions around the financial status of frontier artificial intelligence labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. However, major AI hyperscalers outperformed, with analysts at Vital Knowledge highlighting that these massive technology companies are more likely to fund their ambitions through operating cash flow, a potentially soothing notion as jitters surround a glut of debt-fueled financing deals across the AI industry.
"Our main issue with AI isn’t the technology’s utility or the outlook for token growth but instead OpenAI and Anthropic specifically and whether they can come public on the timelines and at the valuations anticipated by bulls," the Vital Knowledge analysts wrote in a note.
According to media reports, Anthropic, the company behind the popular Claude chatbot, is planning to disclose its third-quarter financial results for the first time later today.
Meanwhile, traders were parsing through an initial batch of bank returns. Shares of JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank, edged down following an unexpected drop in fixed-income trading revenue, while peer Goldman Sachs also ticked lower after its fixed-income revenue missed relative to estimates. Citigroup was the worst performer on the sector-tracking KBW Banks Index, falling by 5.6%.
U.S. inflation data in focus
The marquee event on the economic calendar today will be the unveiling of the monthly U.S. consumer price index, a closely-watched inflation metric.
Overall consumer price growth is expected to have accelerated last month, underlining the inflationary impact of a surge in energy prices and potentially factoring into the trajectory of Federal Reserve monetary policy over the rest of the year.
In the twelve months to September, consumer price growth is tipped to have accelerated to 3.6% from 3.4% previously. Month-on-month, the figure is speeding up to 0.6% from 0.4%.
"This report is likely to be a strong one given the run-up in energy prices over September," analysts at Deutsche Bank said in a note, adding that their economists expect that motor fuel prices soared by 0.6% over the month.
So-called "core" CPI, which strips out volatile items like food and fuel, is projected to stand at 2.5%, up slightly from 2.4% in August. On a monthly basis, the number is expected to slow to 0.2% from 0.3%.
Alternative data compiler Truflation predicted that the "gap between headline and core is widening," as stubbornly elevated energy prices due to an expanding Middle East conflict and aggressive U.S. trade policies threaten renewed goods inflation.
Bank earnings parade
Elsewhere, another host of Wall Street lenders are due to report their quarterly results.
Bank of America posted a fall in third-quarter profit, weighed down by a decision to set aside $1.2 billion in provisions in response to U.S. fines over failures to detect possible illicit activity. Shares slipped in premarket trading.
BlackRock, on the other hand, notched an increase in profit for the period, buoyed by an uptick in fees for managing client funds. The stock rose before the opening bell.
Morgan Stanley also announced a rise in third-quarter income thanks to solid equity trading returns powered by market volatility, although shares edged lower premarket.
The Vital Knowledge analysts said quarterly returns from big banks have not necessarily been "bad," with the numbers appearing to satisfy most expectations, aside from softness in fixed-income trading. However, they flagged a "fear that conditions now are as good as they will get for the industry."
Beyond banks, ASML once again lifted its annual outlook, as the Dutch semiconductor equipment provider gave a rosy picture of soaring AI demand. The company even suggested that clients, which include makers of high-end AI chips, are locking in orders for as far away as 2030. Shares of ASML climbed by more than 1% in European trading.
(Ayushman Ojha contributed reporting)

LONDON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Global stocks rose on Wednesday, helped by a steadying in AI-related shares and government bonds, as investors kept volatility to a minimum ahead of US inflation data later in the day.
Tech shares in Europe were among the top performers of the day, taking their lead from a recovery overnight in Asia, where Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both closed up, and from an upbeat outlook from Dutch chip equipment maker ASML, whose shares rose 1.4%.

"Geopolitics and AI remain the main drivers of the market. There seems to be little progress on the geopolitical front, with a deal looking less likely before the midterms. We have been in the optimistic camp, but have to admit that chances of even a fudge look low," Jefferies strategist Mohit Kumar said.
Government bonds also witnessed some respite after a few weeks of almost non-stop selloffs, in the face of high energy prices and rising expectations for global interest rates to keep edging up.
The yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes dipped 1 basis point to 5.21%, nearing its lowest in two weeks, while 30-year yields were steady at 5.56%, following three days of declines.
Another round of earnings is due from the big banks, starting with Bank of America on Wednesday, which saw profits fall in the third quarter. US bank stocks lost ground on Tuesday after mixed quarterly earnings results from Citigroup and several competitors, which weighed on the broader market.
S&P 500 futures were up 0.1%, while those for the Nasdaq were down 0.2%.
CPI TEST AWAITED
Investors were awaiting the release on Wednesday of the US consumer price index for September, which is expected to have picked up, given the strength of energy and other commodity costs last month.
Economists estimated headline inflation accelerated to an annual 3.6% in September due to rebounding energy prices, with the core CPI rising 0.2% on a monthly basis.
Right now, money markets show traders are attaching a roughly 20% chance of a hike from the Federal Reserve late this month and a near-100% chance of a rise in December. Wednesday’s inflation data could help refine those odds.
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said the Fed may need to raise its policy rate once more this year to slow inflation, but that he saw no need for hikes in 2027.
"With several FOMC members indicating that a pause is likely this month amidst a moderation in job creation, we doubt that inflation numbers would be sufficiently hot to change the odds of hiking materially," Eugene Leow, senior rates strategist at DBS, said in a note.
The dollar index, which tracks the US currency against six others, was up 0.1% at 102.26, close to its highest since April 2025. The euro was down modestly at $1.118, while the pound was steady at $1.326.
Meanwhile, in China, data on Wednesday showed producer prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years while consumer inflation edged up last month, although weak domestic demand kept the increase in broader price pressures contained.

title: IEA cuts 2026 oil demand outlook as diesel crisis, Mideast war disrupt markets
full_text:
ASML shares climb on raised 2026 outlook, capacity expansion plans
Investing.com -- The International Energy Agency (IEA) cut its forecast for global oil demand this year, saying the fallout from the war in the Middle East, including restricted fuel supplies, soaring prices and a weakening economic outlook, is driving the sharpest contraction in years.
World oil demand is expected to fall 2.5 million barrels a day year-over-year in the fourth quarter, with the agency now projecting a 2026 annual decline of 2.6 million barrels a day, steeper than the 2.5 million-barrel-a-day drop forecast last month, citing the Iran war’s disruption and soaring prices. Diesel alone will account for a quarter of the decline.
A partial rebound of 2 million barrels a day in 2027 would still leave global oil use 620,000 barrels a day, or 0.6%, below 2025 levels, IEA said.
IEA said global production rose 2.5 million barrels a day to 102.3 million barrels a day in September, driven by Gulf producers, with OPEC+ gains of 2.1 million barrels a day led by Saudi Arabia. The agency now expects supply to fall by 5.8 million barrels a day for the full year, a slightly steeper decline than the 5.7 million-barrel-a-day drop forecast in its previous report, before rebounding 7.7 million barrels a day in 2027.
"Renewed attacks in the Gulf leave the recovery fragile," the IEA said, warning that the recent escalation threatens September’s recovery in Middle East exports.
Russian production edged up 65,000 barrels a day from August to 8.43 million barrels a day in September, though that remains 870,000 barrels a day below year-ago levels.
The agency now sees world oil supply running 1.73 million barrels a day below demand in 2026, marginally narrower than the 1.74 million-barrel-a-day deficit it projected last month.
Prices have surged as a result of the supply disruptions. North Sea Dated crude jumped $26.17 a barrel in September to $116.89, and was trading around $134 at the time of writing, a 43% increase since the start of September. Brent futures have risen 13% over the same period, to about $107. The IEA pointed to the Sept. 11 bombing of the Saudi East-West Pipeline and a sharp rise in freight rates as key drivers of the rally.
Diesel markets remain under the most acute strain. Global exports fell 700,000 barrels a day year-over-year in September, as losses from Russia and the Middle East outpaced gains elsewhere. Wholesale diesel prices hit all-time highs near $220 a barrel in Europe and the U.S. in September, nearly double crude oil prices.
The IEA said restricted middle distillate supply is "likely to persist well into 2027," and that diesel shortages could continue through that year as well. Russia’s recent easing of diesel export curbs is unlikely to materially alter the global gasoil balance, since the constraints stem from limited Russian refining capacity rather than export policy, the agency added.
Global oil inventories fell 10 million barrels in September, leaving stocks 509 million barrels below pre-war levels. The IEA said markets "may experience more turmoil in the months ahead" absent a resolution to the Middle East conflicts, with any surplus unlikely to emerge before 2027.

The main averages on Wall Street finished lower in the prior session, weighed down in part by lingering questions around the financial status of frontier artificial intelligence labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. Traders were parsing through an initial batch of bank returns as well. U.S. inflation data in focus
The marquee event on the economic calendar today will be the unveiling of the monthly U.S. consumer price index, a closely-watched inflation metric.
Overall consumer price growth is expected to have accelerated last month, underlining the inflationary impact of a surge in energy prices and potentially factoring into the trajectory of Federal Reserve monetary policy over the rest of the year.
In the twelve months to September, consumer price growth is tipped to have accelerated to 3.6% from 3.4% previously. Month-on-month, the figure is speeding up to 0.6% from 0.4%.

So-called "core" CPI, which strips out volatile items like food and fuel, is projected to stand at 2.5%, up slightly from 2.4% in August. On a monthly basis, the number is expected to slow to 0.2% from 0.3%.
Alternative data compiler Truflation predicted that the "gap between headline and core is widening," as stubbornly elevated energy prices due to an expanding Middle East conflict and aggressive U.S. trade policies threaten renewed goods inflation.
Bank earnings parade

BlackRock, on the other hand, notched an increase in profit for the period, buoyed by an uptick in fees for managing client funds. The stock rose before the opening bell.
The Vital Knowledge analysts said that third-quarter returns from big banks have not necessarily been "bad," with the numbers appearing to satisfy most expectations, aside from softness in fixed-income trading. However, they flagged a "fear that conditions now are as good as they will get for the industry."
Beyond banks, ASML once again lifted its annual outlook, as the Dutch semiconductor equipment provider gave a rosy picture of soaring AI demand. The company even suggested that clients, which include makers of high-end AI chips, are locking in orders for as far away as 2030. Shares of ASML climbed by more than 1% in European trading.
Oil climbs
Oil prices ticked higher, as ships were once again targeted in the Strait of Hormuz and renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis spurred more concerns over supply disruptions in the Middle East.
Brent oil futures rose 0.5% to $106.25 a barrel by 07:40 ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 1.9% to $95.88 per barrel.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz also remained constrained after reports this week said more ships have been hit by missiles while attempting to cross the waterway. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations authority said at least two ships were struck in Hormuz on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, worries have abounded that the fighting in the Middle East is now spreading beyond Iran, potentially further constraining Gulf oil supplies.
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched a wave of missiles at Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, targeting major cities, as well as state-owned company Saudi Aramco’s facilities. Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran were struck in the latest attacks, although only a limited fire was reported in the facility.
Gold falls
Gold prices fell. At 06:06 ET, spot gold had fallen 0.6% to $4,138.73 an ounce, while gold futures declined by 0.4% to $4,160.34 an ounce.
Gold has declined for two consecutive sessions, as a flare-up in Middle East attacks raised concerns about further supply disruptions and persistent inflation.
Higher borrowing costs generally weigh on gold because it does not pay interest. The metal has fallen around a fifth from its levels since the U.S.-Iran war erupted in late February, as energy-driven inflation concerns and central bank tightening weighed on prices.

Overall, consumer prices rose 3.7% in the twelve months to September, up from 3.4% in August and faster than expectations of 3.6%. Month-on-month, the closely-watched inflation gauge increased 0.6%, compared to 0.4% previously and in line with forecasts.
Gulf supply constraints due to an expanding conflict in the Middle East drove up energy prices last month, despite reports that supplies out of the region were improving.
The energy portion of the Labor Department’s consumer price index gained 5.2% in September following a 2.1% increase in August. Gasoline prices, in turn, jumped by 9.1%, accounting for over half of the monthly rise in all items, the Labor Department said.

title: Judge extends White House access for CNN, MS NOW, Politico amid legal fight
full_text:

By Jack Queen and Jan Wolfe
WASHINGTON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - A federal judge extended access to the White House for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists, deciding on Tuesday that President Donald Trump likely broke the law when he tried to ban them, in the latest ruling against him in the press freedom dispute.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a written decision that elaborated on his September 24 emergency order that reinstated access for the journalists. The news organizations and press freedom groups have accused Trump of unconstitutional retaliation against journalists for coverage he does not like.
Kelly’s order last month gave the CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists access to the White House grounds on a temporary basis. The judge issued a ruling called a preliminary injunction on Tuesday that will remain in effect until he makes a final judgment in the lawsuit brought by the news organizations, unless an appeals court lifts his order.
Kelly wrote that Trump’s public remarks made clear that he banned the news outlets because he considered their reporting biased and inaccurate, and not because of national security concerns as government lawyers later asserted in court.
"Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination," the judge wrote, adding that "no one should read this decision as suggesting that President Trump’s complaints are meritless."
Trump appointed Kelly in 2017 during his first presidential term.
CAMPAIGN AGAINST THE MEDIA
Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented. He has upended decades of tradition by denying basic access to many major news organizations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He also has filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets.
Trump announced the ban in September on his social media platform, saying CNN, Politico, and MS NOW "shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States." The Justice Department has emphasized Trump’s contention that the ban is legally justified on national security grounds.
The outlets have said the revocation of their White House passes was unlawful retaliation for their news coverage and accused the Trump administration of manufacturing meritless national security concerns to justify the ban.
The outlets said in a lawsuit that the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for freedom of speech and a free press, as well as their rights to due process, meaning fair treatment from the government.
The White House on September 24 reinstated the CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after Kelly decided the ban "likely violated their constitutional due process rights," and ordered their access immediately restored.
’COERCE BETTER COVERAGE’
The judge held a hearing on October 8 to hear arguments by the news outlets and the Justice Department over whether to extend the protection for the journalists against being barred from the White House. The Justice Department defended the bans as fair and justified.
"Here we have the unusual situation where the president himself has said he wants to chill speech. He wants to coerce better coverage," Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told Kelly during the hearing.
"CNN, MS NOW and Politico engaged in apparently indefensible conduct," Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik said.
The legal battle is being waged just weeks before the November 3 US midterm elections in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. Trump’s job approval ratings are at record lows in opinion polls amid concerns over issues such as inflation and the Iran war.

NEW YORK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter, according to an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting with Anthropic leadership in San Francisco on Wednesday.
Revenue in the first quarter was $4.7 billion, and $11.6 billion in the second quarter, according to the person who attended the investor day meant to familiarize prospective Anthropic investors before its highly anticipated IPO. Scrutiny of AI companies’ finances has intensified as they pour money into chips, data centers and computing power needed to develop and operate increasingly powerful models.
Targeting a valuation of over $2 trillion, Anthropic is seeking to convince investors that its breakneck revenue growth can eventually outrun the enormous costs of building and running AI systems.
Last year, Anthropic’s revenue increased twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion, even as the company lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis, excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising, Reuters reported exclusively last month.
The company has committed at least $518 billion over a decade for cloud services, computing and infrastructure.
Founded by former OpenAI executives, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models. Its expansion has been underpinned by Alphabet’s Google and Amazon, which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors.
Anthropic has also sought to distinguish itself through its focus on AI safety, warning of the dangers posed by increasingly capable systems even as it competes in the race to develop and commercialize more powerful models.
Its research has found that its own AI agents have engaged in troubling behavior in test environments, including leaking sensitive information and sabotaging code, though the company has said it has not seen evidence of such misalignment in real-world deployments.
